u>0$ there is a smooth, compactly supported field $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}u_0=0$ for which no pair $u:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$, $p:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ has all of the following properties: joint smoothness up to $t=0$ on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$; $u(0)=u_0$; $\partial_tu+(u\cdot

abla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ for every $t>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$; and one finite constant $A$ with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx\le A$ for every $t\ge0$. The single bound is uniform over the entire half-line, not a separate bound on each finite interval. The integral is the nonnegative integral, so an infinite energy cannot satisfy the inequality. A real upper bound is converted to its nonnegative part, which does not alter existence of a finite bound. Functions are defined also for negative times, but no condition is imposed there. This statement gives no blow-up time, trajectory, rate, or profile-comparison estimate.

The formal statement specifies the whole-space failure of a global smooth solution with one uniform energy bound; it does not formulate the historical regularity problem or a finite blow-up trajectory.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators, with $C$ compact. Let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ and $\|T_0\|\le b$, and write $T=T_0+C$. This assertion says that there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$, and a bounded projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$, whose range is finite-dimensional, such that $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$ for every natural number $n$ and every $x\in\mathcal X$. The restriction of $T$ maps the range of $P_u$ onto itself. Hence the complement has a controlled forward evolution and the finite-dimensional part has a controlled inverse evolution. The inequalities imply $r_2>0$, so the reciprocal in $r_2^{-n}$ is an ordinary reciprocal. The formulation uses projections and powers rather than a list of complex eigenvalues. It does not impose the existence or size of an unstable eigenvalue. Taking $b=\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$ is the application to the period map.

The formal assertion provides a finite-dimensional commuting projection for every compact perturbation of a small bounded operator, without assuming a particular unstable eigenvalue; it is the spectral input rather than the nonlinear stability conclusion.
rows.name: Breakdown.DichotomyHolds
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.DichotomyHolds` supplies the finite-rank commuting projection for a compact perturbation of a bounded operator with small norm. Forward powers decay faster on the complement than inverse powers can grow on the projected space. The separation underlies the choice of finitely many corrections to the datum.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.

The correction component of the linear right inverse lies in a fixed finite-dimensional space; nonlinear stability and the physical norm identification require the subsequent contraction and realization.

The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The conjugate symmetry is the reality condition and $n\cdot a(n)=0$ is the divergence-free condition. At $n=0$ the latter gives no restriction, which is why nonzero constants are included. The space is a closed real subspace of $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and is complete. A nonzero constant has positive formal norm and zero gradient norm, so the mean-zero restriction is essential in (3.16). Equation (3.15) instead uses the homogeneous norm on mean-zero fields of arbitrary period $L$. The distinction matters: the zero Fourier mode contributes to the formal norm, and no variable spatial period is a parameter of an element of the formal space.

The formal periodic space uses the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm on the fixed unit torus and permits a nonzero mean.

For finite real numbers $a,b$, a curve $u$ defined for all real times with values in this periodic space is a mild solution on $[a,b)$ if it is continuous there and, for every $t\in[a,b)$, the integral $\int_a^tK_{\mathbb T}(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ is Bochner integrable in the formal periodic space and $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK_{\mathbb T}(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Here the heat operator has Fourier multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2(t-a)|n|^2}$, and $K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)$ is the symmetrized projected transport operator for $\tau>0$, with value zero for $\tau\le0$. No behavior at $b$ or outside $[a,b)$ is required. This definition concerns the unit torus with its inhomogeneous norm, whereas §3.6 works in mean-zero homogeneous spaces at arbitrary period.

The same Duhamel form is imposed on a curve in that larger periodic Fourier space; zero mean is not part of the condition.

Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

A separate theorem proves this statement from the spectral dichotomy.

Let $V$ be the real Hilbert space of unit-periodic solenoidal Fourier states, with norm squared $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat u(k)|^2$; zero mean is not required. Assume $\|\bar u_n(s)\|\ge c_0$ for all $n,s$, $\sup_s\|z_n(s)\|\le Z$ for all $n$, and $u_n=\bar u_n+\theta^n z_n$. Put $a_n=T-T\lambda^n$ and $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$. On $[a_n,a_{n+1})$, define the joined curve by $U(t)=\mu_n^{-1/4}u_n((t-a_n)/\mu_n)$. The formal statement concludes that $\{\|U(t)\|:0\le t<T\}$ is unbounded above. The powers $\lambda^n$ and $\theta^n$ have nonnegative integer exponents. The positive parameters ensure that all divisions and logarithms used to select the interval are legitimate on $[0,T)$. Continuous pieces are extended by their endpoint values when evaluated outside their interval; these values are irrelevant on the stated pieces. No matching of endpoints or mild equation is assumed here, so neither continuity of $U$ nor its being a solution is part of this conclusion. This is a geometric unboundedness criterion, stated as a proposition; its proof is a separate theorem.

For $\mu>0$, assume strongly continuous dilations satisfying $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For every $f$ in a dense subset of $X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with these operators at all their defined real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For every $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to converge and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. The formal space $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ consisting of classes $g$ such that $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The first condition represents a real velocity; the second represents zero divergence. The interpretation for a physical velocity $u$ is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, with the Fourier convention $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. Thus the norm on the formal space is $\|g\|_2$, corresponding to $\|\nabla u\|_2$. Elements are classes modulo equality almost everywhere, with no smoothness imposed. The denominator in the longitudinal projection is $|\xi|^2$; its reciprocal is assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which does not affect an $L^2$ class. The paper defines $X$ as divergence-free physical fields in $L^6$ with gradient in $L^2$. Identifying that description with this Fourier space requires the reconstruction and density results. This definition by itself does not assert the paper's completion theorem for all fields.

**Lemma 3.3.** Let $a\le b$, and let $u,v:[a,b]\to\mathcal X$ be continuous. Then for every $t\in[a,b]$ the map $t'\mapsto K(t-t')(u(t'),v(t'))$ is integrable on $[a,t]$, and the map $$
t\mapsto\int_a^t K(t-t')(u(t'),v(t'))\,dt'
$$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.

assessments.fidelity_note: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau)$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps, continuous for each fixed pair of arguments when $\tau>0$. Assume $G(s)K(\tau)(u,v)=K(s+\tau)(u,v)$ for $s\ge0,\tau>0$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. If $a\le b$ and $u,v$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, with $\|u(s)\|\le M$ and $\|v(s)\|\le N$ throughout, then $I(t)=\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),v(s))\,ds$ is Bochner integrable for every $t\in[a,b]$ and continuous in $t$. When $t-a\le1$, $\|I(t)\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Such $M,N$ exist by compactness. This includes Lemma 3.3 and an additional short-time estimate under a weaker lag-bound hypothesis. This linked definition states the assertion.

For $T>0$, the formal assertion identifies $B_T:C([0,T];\mathcal X)^2\to C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ by $B_T(f,h)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds$ and proves bounded bilinearity; $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. assessments.fidelity_note: Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry of the real Hilbert space $X$. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. assessments.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. Fix an integer $k\ge1$, set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$, and define $a_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ for $0\le\sigma\le L$. The formal assertion states that $a_n$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,L]$, $D_\mu a_n(L)=a_{n+1}(0)$ and $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$. If $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$, it also states $\|a_n\|_\infty\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. The paper's formula instead holds on a whole period for every $0\le\sigma<1$: $u^*(1-\lambda^n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\rho_R^nD_{\lambda^{-n}}u^*(\sigma)$, $\lambda=e^{-S}$. The formal assertion states matching and a one-period shift for the short pieces, without that whole-period identity as a conclusion.

assessments.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. For a dense linear subspace $C\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the formal assertion chooses $k\ge1$, $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu\le t_0$ and $\mu^{1/4}<\theta<1$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with its supremum norm, set $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. It gives $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, a finite-dimensional $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C$, and a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. Writing $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, the conclusions are $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$; its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The paper's correction space is represented by $J(V)$ when $C$ consists of smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields. rows.annotation: `Breakdown.orbitBound` gives a uniform upper bound on the continuous recurrent orbit. In the physical variable it becomes the upper $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ estimate by the $\dot H^1$ dilation law. The positive lower bound uses nonvanishing and a separate result.

assessments.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. The theorem supplies $c>0$ with $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every real $s$. Dilation gives $\|u^*(t)\|\ge c(1-t)^{-1/4}$ for $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$, $0\le t<1$. The uniform upper bound and hence the complete two-sided assertion (4.4) are separate.

assessments.fidelity_note: In $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, with norm $\|u\|_X=\|\nabla u\|_2$, the formal assertion requires, for $\mu,\eta>0$, $\|D_\mu x\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$ and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$. Here $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$ and $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$. At $\mu=(1-t)^{-1}$, $t<1$, this gives the factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$. For $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$, the two-sided estimate (4.4) also needs positive lower and finite upper bounds for $\|w(s)\|$. Neither orbit bound is part of this formal assertion.

On the frequency-side model of $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ used in the formalization, $D_\mu$ acts by $f(\xi)\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}f(\mu^{-1/2}\xi)$, which corresponds to the paper's $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$, and $G(t)$ multiplies by $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$. The formal statement asserts, for $\mu,\eta>0$, $\|D_\mu x\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and that $D_\mu$ is given by this frequency formula. At $\mu=(1-t)^{-1}$, $t<1$, this gives the factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$. For $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$, the two-sided estimate (4.4) also needs positive lower and finite upper bounds for $\|w(s)\|$. Neither orbit bound is part of this formal assertion.

assessments.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Fix an integer $k\ge1$, put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu$ and $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$ on $[0,L]$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ define $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$ and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. The formal assertion assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every $n$, and states that $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$. With $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$, $\mathcal M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$ and $\mathcal M_0=\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k$, it states $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, compactness of $\mathcal M-\mathcal M_0$, and $\|\mathcal M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}$. The heat-scaling law gives $(D_\mu G(L))^k=D_{e^{-S}}G(1-e^{-S})$, so the free operator and the constant agree with Lemma 4.4. The formal statement also assumes the positive subdivision and $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every short piece. It does not state the separate identification of its product with the paper's whole-period trajectory. Thus the displayed conclusions correspond after additional identifications, while the full statements have different hypotheses and formulations.

Fix an integer $k\ge1$, set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$, and define $a_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ for $0\le\sigma\le L$. The formal assertion states that $a_n$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,L]$, $D_\mu a_n(L)=a_{n+1}(0)$ and $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$. If $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$, it also states $\|a_n\|_\infty\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. The paper proves the whole-period identity by induction on $n$ and uses $\lambda=e^{-S}$. The formal assertion instead expresses the corresponding recurrence on the subdivision $S/k$ and gives no whole-period induction formula as a stated conclusion.

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\mu<1$ and continuous curves $a_n:[0,1-\mu]\to X$ in a real Hilbert space with dilations $D_\mu$, the formal reconstruction is $v(t)=D_{\mu^{-n}}a_n(\sigma)$, $n=\lfloor\log(1-t)/\log\mu\rfloor_{\mathbb N}$ and $\sigma=(t-(1-\mu^n))/\mu^n$. On $0\le t<1$ this gives $0\le\sigma<1-\mu$ and $1-t=\mu^n(1-\sigma)$. The natural-number floor is zero on negative inputs. Outside each interval a curve is extended by its endpoint value. With $\mu=\lambda=e^{-S}$, $S>0$, the selected index and local time are the $n,\sigma$ in the paper. The linked item defines the selected curve; the interval-membership and reconstruction identities are proved in the separate joining result. This definition is not itself that existence theorem.

assessments.fidelity_note: For a real normed space $X$ and real $L$, the formal object is $C([0,L];X)$ with its ordinary supremum norm; it is Banach when $X$ is complete. It contains no parameter $\kappa$. The paper's $C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ uses the finite norm $\sup_{0\le t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|$. The two domains and norms differ; the formal interval construction introduces geometric weights through a sequence of rescaled curves.

assessments.fidelity_note: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real $\theta$, a prescribed source sequence $c_n$ and an initial value $x_0$, the formal definition is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n$. It has no boundedness or decay conclusion. At $\theta=0$ division is assigned zero; the dichotomy arguments impose $\theta>0$. The paper's formula (4.5) defines a space of continuous curves with a weighted supremum norm on $[0,1)$. The recurrence definition contains no such function space or norm. In applications, geometric normalization of an already given sequence is one part of the interval construction.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. Assume $K(\tau)(f,g)$ depends continuously on $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)(f,g)=K(s+\tau)(f,g)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $0<T\le1$, $a,v\in C([0,T];X)$ and $x\in X$. Write $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$. If $a(t)=G(t)a(0)+B_T(a,a)(t)$ and $v(t)=G(t)x+2B_T(a,v)(t)+B_T(v,v)(t)$, the formal assertion concludes $v(0)=x$ and $a+v$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,T]$, including integrability of its Duhamel term. The quoted paper assertion is an equivalence on $[0,1)$. The formal assertion gives the implication from the perturbation identity to an exact mild sum on a closed interval of length at most one; it does not state the converse.

rows.fidelity_note: The linked theorem takes the spectral dichotomy assertion as a premise: compact perturbations of small operators on real Hilbert spaces admit a commuting finite-rank projection with geometric forward and inverse bounds. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. For a dense linear subspace $C\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the formal assertion chooses $k\ge1$, $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu\le t_0$ and $\mu^{1/4}<\theta<1$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with its supremum norm, set $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. It gives $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, a finite-dimensional $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C$, and a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. Writing $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, the conclusions are $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$; its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The paper's correction space is represented by $J(V)$ when $C$ consists of smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields. The formal conclusion controls the bounded sequence norm and the coordinate $e$; it does not state the map $C_\kappa\to E\times C_\kappa$ of Proposition 4.3.

On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ put $B_n(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK_n(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ and $\Gamma_nx(t)=G_n(t)x$. Assume $a_n,r_n\in Y$, $\sup_n\|a_n\|_Y<\infty$, $a_n=\Gamma_na_n(0)+B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n$, $\|r_n\|_Y\le\theta^n\rho$, and $a_{n+1}(0)=c\,a_n(L)$. For bounded linear $J:E\to X$, require a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to E\times\ell^\infty(Y)$ which sends $g$ to $(e,z)$ satisfying $z_0-2B_0(a_0,z_0)-\Gamma_0Je=g_0$ and $z_n-2B_n(a_n,z_n)-(c/\theta)\Gamma_nz_{n-1}(L)=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, the formal assertion supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The formal assertion requires a normed complete correction space $E$ and a bounded inverse controlling both components. In Lemma 4.8, $E$ is only a vector space and the bound is imposed on the curve component alone. The formal source norm also separates residual and datum displacement. These differences prevent identification of this assertion with the full global lemma.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. Fix an integer $k\ge1$, put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu$ and $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$ on $[0,L]$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ define $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$ and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. The formal assertion assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every $n$, and states that $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$. With $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$, $\mathcal M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$ and $\mathcal M_0=\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k$, it states $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, compactness of $\mathcal M-\mathcal M_0$, and $\|\mathcal M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}$. The formal assertion assumes the supplied subdivision and its small-operator bounds. It does not choose $k$. The paper instead defines the bounded inverse $\mathcal U$ of $h\mapsto h-2\mathcal B(u^*,h)$ over the entire first period $[0,1-e^{-S}]$, without first presenting a subdivision.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $k\ge1$, $\theta>0$, and let $\rho:X\to X$ be a surjective linear isometry. Let $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$, $E:Y\to X$ and $J,P:X\to X$ be bounded linear maps. Assume $I-A_n$ have uniformly bounded inverses. Set $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$ and $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$, and assume $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $P^2=P$, $PM=MP$, $PJ=P$. For $0\le r_1<\theta^k<r_2$, require $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$, $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for all $n\ge0,x\in X$, and surjectivity of $M$ on $\operatorname{ran}P$. The formal assertion supplies a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. For $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, it states $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The product norm is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. The previous-endpoint term $\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}$ is the formal recurrence coupling. The paper derives the specific continuous-time restart formula for $v-g$ by subtracting its Duhamel identities. The formal assertion takes the interval maps as inputs and does not prove that restart formula for a global forced curve.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal space $X$ is a frequency-side model of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$: a closed subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ of transverse fields with the reality symmetry, on which $G(t)$ is the multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$ and $D_\mu$ acts by $f(\xi)\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}f(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$, the frequency form of $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. For $\mu,\eta>0$ the formal assertion states $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and agreement of $D_\mu$ with the dilation on $L^2$. For natural $n$, $\lambda=e^{-S}>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, set $\mu=\lambda^n$ and $t=\sigma$ to obtain $D_{\lambda^n}G(\lambda^n\sigma)=G(\sigma)D_{\lambda^n}$. Commutation with $\rho_R$ and the identification of the rescaled initial vector are additional steps in the paper's equation. They are not components of this dilation assertion.

ties.name: Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp
ties.plain: The linearized interaction on a piece

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. For $k\ge1$ and $L=1-e^{-S/k}$, the formal interaction is $A_nv(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),v(r))\,dr$, with $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$. The kernel-scaling identity is an assumption of the surrounding mathematical setting. The definition of $A_n$ does not itself assert the change of variables from a global forced solution or the whole-period formula printed here.

rows.plain: The linearized interaction on a piece
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp` defines the linearized interaction on a rescaled interval by integrating $2K(t-r)(a_n(r),v(r))$, where $a_n$ is the reference piece. Applying the kernel-scaling identity identifies it with the period operator in the paper.

rows.fidelity_note: For real normed spaces $X,Y$ and bounded linear maps $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$, $E:Y\to X$, the formal definition is $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$. An operator without a bounded inverse is assigned inverse zero. If $I-A_n$ is invertible, $(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma x$ solves the linear interval equation, and $S_nx$ is its rescaled endpoint. In the application $Y=C([0,L];X)$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. When $I-A_n$ is invertible, the corresponding interval trajectory with a source is $(I-A_n)^{-1}(\Gamma\chi+g)$. The formal definition here applies $E$ only to the homogeneous trajectory $(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma\chi$. It states neither the inhomogeneous trajectory identity nor the paper's unsplit decomposition on $[0,1-e^{-S}]$.

ties.plain: The future tail satisfies the recurrence

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space and $N,M,P:X\to X$ bounded and linear with $PN=N$ and $MN=P$. Assume $0<\Theta<r_2$, $A\ge0$, $\|N^{j+1}x\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|x\|$ for every natural $j$ and $x\in X$, and $\|c_j\|\le R$ for all $j$, so that $U(c)=-\sum_{j\ge0}\Theta^jN^{j+1}c_j$ converges. This theorem does not identify $c_j$ with the source derived from a global solution, and it does not supply the complementary finite sum.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. rows.fidelity_note: Let $X,E$ be real Banach spaces, $0<L\le1$, $0<\theta<1$, $c\in\mathbb R$, and $C_K\ge0$. Suppose a bounded linear map $R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to\mathcal X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$ solves the linear problem: if $R g=(e,z)$, then $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for every $n\ge1$. $\displaystyle \partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0.$

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume the radial-potential assertion that every smooth solenoidal $g$ has a smooth potential $A_{x_0,g}$ with $\operatorname{curl}A_{x_0,g}=g$. For every smooth scalar function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, every centre $x_0$ and every smooth solenoidal vector field $g$, the formal statement then proves that $\bar g=\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A_{x_0,g}$ is smooth and $\nabla\cdot\bar g=0$ at every point. Here $A_{x_0,g}(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(x_0+\sigma(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,d\sigma$. In §5 take $x_0=0$, $g=u^*(t)$ and $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$ with $r>0$. This theorem assumes no support or size conditions on $\chi$ and therefore gives no support radius, no equality on an inner ball, and no norm bound. Its radial-potential premise is proved in the preceding curl theorem.

The formal statement proves smoothness and zero divergence for an arbitrary smooth cutoff, with no support or inner-agreement conclusion.

assessments.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, with $\operatorname{div}W=0$ and
$\displaystyle \partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0.$
Assume one constant $C$ bounds $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, for every real $s$ and every $y$. Recurrence and nonvanishing are unnecessary here. The first-derivative operator norm differs from the paper's Frobenius norm by a factor at most $\sqrt3$.

For $A_s(y)=\int_0^1\sigma W(s,\sigma y)\times y\,d\sigma$, the formal theorem proves $|A_s(y)|\le C$ for every real $s$ and every $y$. Smoothness makes this integral the ordinary radial integral. Under the physical change of variables $y=x/\sqrt{1-t}$, the potential of $(1-t)^{-1/2}W(-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ is $A_{-\log(1-t)}(y)$.

The formal bound is $|A_s(y)|\le C$ for the potential of the similarity profile; the physical potential equals $A_s((1-t)^{-1/2}x)$, which preserves the bound.

rows.fidelity_note:
Fix $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and the smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For an arbitrary function $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and real $T,t$ with $t<T$, put $\ell=T-t>0$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Form $\bar u=\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A_g$ with the radial potential about $a$, and let $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell y)$. The formal statement proves $f(y)=\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)W(s,y)+\sqrt\ell\,\nabla\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)\times\int_0^1\sigma W(s,\sigma y)\times y\,d\sigma$. No smoothness, equation or decay of $W$ is assumed, and the only time hypothesis is $t<T$. If $T=0$, division by zero is taken to be zero and $\log0=0$; for a negative logarithm argument the formal real logarithm is the logarithm of its absolute value. For the intended case $T>0$, every logarithm and square root has a positive argument. Nonintegrable vector integrals are assigned zero, so this purely algebraic identity is stated even for inputs for which the potential is not an ordinary integral.

The formal expanded formula is for a cutoff after translation and dilation to similarity coordinates; its radius is $1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$ and its inner radius is half as large.

The formal statement proves that $h$ is integrable and that $\int h(y)\,dy\le3|B_1|(2a^2+b\rho^2)\rho$, where $|B_1|=4\pi/3$ is the volume of the unit ball. The estimate is a deliberately nonsharp bound obtained from the radial integral. The denominator $1+|y|$ is always positive, including at zero. The assertion supplies the integrability and radius dependence used to estimate the $L^2$ norm of the cutoff. It does not identify the cutoff field or state the paper's exact integral with $|x|^{-2}$; those enter through a separate pointwise comparison.

Let $Z$ be a complete normed abelian group, let $b,K\ge0$ satisfy $8Kb\le1$, and let $G:Z\to Z$ obey
$\displaystyle \|G(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2,\qquad \|G(z)-G(w)\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$
for all $z,w$. The formal lemma gives a fixed point $G(z)=z$ with $\|z\|\le2b$. No time variable, velocity space, or finite-dimensional correction space is part of this abstract statement.

assessments.fidelity_note:
This theorem assumes the following analytic representation facts. On the unit torus, every $C^1$ periodic vector field satisfies $\widehat{\partial_jf}(k)=2\pi i k_j\widehat f(k)$. A smooth compactly supported solenoidal field transplanted at $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$ is smooth, unit-periodic, solenoidal, and agrees with its unwrapped dilation on the ball of radius $1/4$ about $(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. The whole-space heat operators form a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup for nonnegative time and act by the multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2\max(t,0)|\xi|^2}$ on their Fourier representatives.

The proof also assumes: uniformly bounded measurable matrix multipliers after any invertible real linear frequency change have their stated almost-everywhere $L^2$ action; the direct and inverse $L^2$ Fourier transforms agree with the corresponding integrals on $L^1\cap L^2$; real $L^2$ fields have conjugate-symmetric Fourier transforms; and, when $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere for solenoidal representatives, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ equals the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. The main construction supplies these analytic facts before using this theorem.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal field $\varphi$, and every $b,\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$ and $0\le\tau\le\varepsilon^{-1}$, the local-data norm of the difference between the restrictions of $e^{\tau\Delta}\varphi$ and $\mu^{1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\varphi_\mu$ is at most $\delta$. This is uniform convergence on a bounded time interval, including time zero. The threshold can depend on $\varphi$ and no bound proportional to $\|\varphi\|_1$ is asserted. Formula (6.3) instead gives a uniform explicit $L^{-5/2}$ estimate for all $t>0$.

The formal assertion gives an error at most any prescribed $\delta$ for sufficiently small scale, uniformly on $[0,\varepsilon^{-1}]$ for each fixed datum. It does not give the all-positive-time rate $CL^{-5/2}\|f\|_1$.

ties.name: Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties_holds
ties.plain: Support and agreement of the cutoff

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ and $\nabla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\rm op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $\chi$ be the fixed smooth cutoff with $0\le\chi\le1$, equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, set $\ell=T-t$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Define $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, $\bar u(x)=\chi(x)g(x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A_g(x)$, and $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell\,y)$. Thus $f$ is the cutoff expressed in similarity coordinates; its inner and outer radii are $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ and $1/(8\sqrt\ell)$. Put $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ and $\bar p(x)=\chi(x)\ell^{-1}[q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$.

For every $T>0$, the formal statement proves that $(t,x)\mapsto\bar u(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$, is divergence-free, vanishes for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and equals $g$ for $|x-a|\le1/16$. It also proves smoothness and the same outer support for $\bar p(t,x)=\chi(x)[\ell^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-\ell^{-1}q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$, where $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ is fixed. Thus each spatial cutoff is in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. The centre, radii, time interval and pressure normalization are fixed as stated; an arbitrary radius $r$ is absent from the assertion. All logarithms, square roots and quotients used for $t<T$, $T>0$ have their ordinary positive arguments. The result gives no quantitative norm estimate.

The formal theorem applies the solenoidal cutoff after scaling to the unit cell: it agrees with the centered self-similar field on radius $1/16$ and vanishes outside radius $1/8$, for all $t<T$. The paper states the corresponding radii $L/16,L/8$ on the large torus.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. 

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero. 

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space. 

An approximation on $[0,\ell]$ is specified, for every integer $n\ge0$, by a finite sum $A_n(s)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_{n,j}(s)\varphi_{n,j}$, where each $\alpha_{n,j}$ is continuous, each $\varphi_{n,j}$ is smooth, compactly supported and solenoidal with support in $\bar B_b$, and both the weights and $\|\varphi_{n,j}\|_X$ have one uniform bound. The number $m$ is fixed. 

Use the whole-space heat flow, Navier–Stokes bilinear kernel and spatial dilation $D_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{1/2}f(\lambda^{1/2}x)$, and assume the periodic kernel estimate $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\le C_{\mathbb T}\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $P>0$, let $k>0$ be an integer, put $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$ and $\ell=1-\lambda\le1/2$, and choose $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ and $b>0$. The preceding finite-sum approximation is taken on $[0,\ell]$. Let $E$ be finite dimensional, let $J:E\to X$ be bounded linear, and let $e\mapsto\psi_e$ be linear, with each $\psi_e$ smooth, compactly supported, solenoidal, supported in $\bar B_b$, and representing $Je$.

The three spaces used below are the bounded sequences of continuous $X$-valued, periodic-$H^1$-valued and local-data-valued curves on $[0,\ell]$. Each has norm $\sup_n\sup_{0\le s\le\ell}\|v_n(s)\|$. Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, let $w$ reduce coordinates to the unit cell centered at $a$, and put $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$. The periodic datum map is $J_{\mathbb T}e=T^{1/4}(\psi_e)_T$, where $(\psi_e)_T(x)=T^{-1/2}\psi_e((w(x)-a)/\sqrt T)$.

Here are the operators whose differences the formal statement controls. Whole-space restriction $R$ records $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv_n$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v_n$. Periodic restriction $R_{\mathbb T}$ records $1_{\bar B_b}\mu_n^{3/4}\partial_jz_n(a+\sqrt{\mu_n}y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu_n^{1/4}z_n(a+\sqrt{\mu_n}y)$. The periodic restriction is zero if $0<\mu_n\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt{\mu_n}b\le1/8$ fail; sufficiently small $T$ ensures these conditions. For a local tuple $\zeta=(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ put $F_{\varphi,\zeta}=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$. The whole-space interaction is
$\displaystyle (B\zeta)_n(s)=-\sum_l\int_0^s\alpha_{n,l}(\sigma)e^{(s-\sigma)\Delta}\mathbb PF_{\varphi_{n,l},\zeta_n(\sigma)}\,d\sigma.$
For $B_{\mathbb T}$ replace the projected heat field under the integral by
$\displaystyle \mu_n^{-1/4}e^{\mu_n(s-\sigma)\Delta}\mathbb P\bigl[F_{\varphi_{n,l},\zeta_n(\sigma)}((w(x)-a)/\sqrt{\mu_n})\bigr].$
The minus sign and weights are unchanged. These definitions use the bounded integral operators supplied by the heat estimates; their general definitions assign zero if the required bounded realization does not exist.

The preceding-interval maps satisfy $(Sy)_0=(S_{\mathbb T}z)_0=0$ and, for $n\ge1$,
$\displaystyle (Sy)_n(s)=\theta^{-1}e^{s\Delta}D_\lambda y_{n-1}(\ell),\qquad (S_{\mathbb T}z)_n(s)=\frac{\lambda^{1/4}}\theta e^{\mu_ns\Delta}z_{n-1}(\ell).$
The datum maps have $(Ge)_0(s)=e^{s\Delta}Je$ and $(G_{\mathbb T}e)_0(s)=e^{Ts\Delta}J_{\mathbb T}e$, with all later entries zero. The propagation bounds are $\|S\|,\|S_{\mathbb T}\|\le\lambda^{1/4}/\theta<1$, so $I-S$ and $I-S_{\mathbb T}$ have ordinary bounded inverses. The general inverse convention assigns zero to a noninvertible operator, which is excluded here.

For every $\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts a $T_0>0$ such that, for every $0<T\le1$ with $T<T_0$, and the datum map just specified,
$\displaystyle \|R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}B_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}B\|\le\delta,\qquad \|R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}G_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}G\|\le\delta.$
The threshold is uniform in the sequence index. No explicit rate in $T$ or the paper’s large torus period is asserted.

This theorem assumes the following analytic representation facts. On the unit torus, every $C^1$ periodic vector field satisfies $\widehat{\partial_jf}(k)=2\pi i k_j\widehat f(k)$. A smooth compactly supported solenoidal field transplanted at $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$ is smooth, unit-periodic, solenoidal, and agrees with its unwrapped dilation on the ball of radius $1/4$ about $(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. The whole-space heat operators form a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup for nonnegative time and act by the multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2\max(t,0)|\xi|^2}$ on their Fourier representatives.

The proof also assumes: uniformly bounded measurable matrix multipliers after any invertible real linear frequency change have their stated almost-everywhere $L^2$ action; the direct and inverse $L^2$ Fourier transforms agree with the corresponding integrals on $L^1\cap L^2$; real $L^2$ fields have conjugate-symmetric Fourier transforms; and, when $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere for solenoidal representatives, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ equals the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. The main construction supplies these analytic facts before using this theorem.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal field $\varphi$, and every $b,\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$ and $0\le\tau\le\varepsilon^{-1}$, the local-data norm of the difference between the restrictions of $e^{\tau\Delta}\varphi$ and $\mu^{1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\varphi_\mu$ is at most $\delta$. Formula (6.3) instead gives a uniform explicit $L^{-5/2}$ estimate for all $t>0$.

merged.quote: **Proposition B.1.** For data of the form of Subsection B.1 and weights of the form above, let $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, and let the weights be admissible at $\alpha$. Let $v\in\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}^\Gamma$, $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$ and $F\in\mathcal H$ be such that $F\simeq\mathcal T_{S(\alpha)}v+\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r}v+\sum_i\beta_i b_i$.

assessments.fidelity_note: The formal theorem admits measurable periodic perturbations with weak derivatives and square-integrable transport and right-hand side; at $c=3/50,w=39/50$ the paper’s class is a special case of this larger analytic class.

The formal theorem contains Proposition B.1 after $c=3/50$ and $w=w_{0}=39/50$ are substituted. It also applies to periodic weak perturbations and arbitrary measurable periodic $L^{2}$ right-hand sides, and to admissible analytic data without the particular piecewise-polynomial representations of B.1. The stronger verdict concerns these larger admitted classes and parameters; the specialized conclusions and constant agree with the proposition.

Fix $S>0$, $\Gamma$, $0<c,c_\mu <1$, a bounded measurable axisymmetric $w\ge w_{0}>0$, and admissible weights and reference bounds of B.2: nonnegative Lipschitz $\lambda ,\mu$ with the specified decay, positive measurable axisymmetric auxiliary functions, $C^{2}$ even weights D,Z with their derivative bounds, positive $\Omega _p$ on each selected set, (B.19), and $I'_{2}\ge 0$. assessments.fidelity_note: The algebraic identity identifies N with the sum of cell, rectangle and global forms; it supplies no density upper bound. abla G,
abla U,F,q$, it requires $|U|\lesssim(1+r)^{-1}$, $|\Delta G|\lesssim(1+r)^{-4}$ and $|\Delta U|\lesssim(1+r)^{-3}$, the last two almost everywhere in space. The paper does not state the first bound and bounds both Laplacians by $Cr^{-1}(1+r)^{-2}$. Its pressure-gradient decay is encoded by $r|
abla q|\le C$ and $r^3|
abla q|\le C$, which gives the same near-origin and far-field orders away from $r=0$, up to changing the constant. These weighted inequalities do not restrict the derivative at the origin. The formal hypothesis therefore differs in the derivative requirements and in the precise decay bounds.

The formal condition requires $\mathsf G_j$ and $\mathsf U_j$ to be jointly $C^1$ with weak second derivatives on every time slice, and $\mathsf F_j$ and $q_j$ to be measurable with distributional divergence and gradient. Besides the displayed bounds on $\mathsf G_j$, $

abla q_j|\le C$ and $|y|^3|

rows.fidelity_note: The residual norm bound uses one threshold for every certified parameter. This is the uniform verification input, separate from the paper’s exploratory fitting diagnostic.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l2
rows.note: The residual norm bound uses one threshold for every certified parameter. This is the uniform verification input, separate from the paper’s exploratory fitting diagnostic.
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l2` requires one bound on the $L^2$ norm of $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The exploratory residual at the fitted parameter provides no such uniform estimate.

rows.fidelity_note: The sampled residual row bounds also use one budget uniformly over the certified parameter set.
rows.name: Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_rows
rows.note: The sampled residual row bounds also use one budget uniformly over the certified parameter set.
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_rows` imposes the bounds on the specified residual row pairings for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. These uniform row bounds are an additional certificate input beyond the residual norm.

rows.name: Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsStrongRightSide
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsStrongRightSide` states the continuum residual formula almost everywhere using the perturbation’s weak derivatives, the reference field, forcing and pressure gradient. Under the identification of those derivative slots, this is the linearized expression in the passage. The discretized derivative matrix is a separate object.

assessments.fidelity_note: When the supplied matrix is the gradient of $v$, the formal definition gives these same two terms, in the opposite order of addition.

rows.name: Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.couplingField
rows.annotation: If the supplied matrix is $\nabla v$, its curl represents $\operatorname{curl}v$. The coupling field then adds $(\operatorname{curl}v)\times W$ and $(\operatorname{curl}W)\times v$, the two first-order coupling terms of (C.2).

rows.name: Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.affineField
rows.note: The represented affine field is the center profile plus the coefficient-weighted tangent fields.
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.affineField` forms the affine field from the center and the parameter-weighted tangent directions at fixed phase. In the ball where $f_*=0$, the varying-phase expression (B.9) agrees with this affine form.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition calculates the shifted frequency from the time harmonic, angular harmonic and frame rotation rate.
rows.name: Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq
rows.note: The formal definition calculates the shifted frequency from the time harmonic, angular harmonic and frame rotation rate.
rows.annotation: `Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq` computes $2\pi\iota_1/P+a\iota_2$ from the temporal harmonic, angular harmonic, period and frame rate. Substituting the two frame rates and their mode indices gives the frequencies displayed in the passage.
